title: Case study: flash sale
objective: Run a flash sale: never sell stock you don't have, and let shoppers in at a rate the database can take, neither too fast nor too slow.

sources.title: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications (O'Reilly, 2017), chapter 7: preventing lost updates
Cloudflare Docs: Waiting Room (queues surges of visitors so they don't overload the origin)

simplifies: A generic design. The simulation reuses the train-booking model, so items in stock are shown as "seats". Database capacity (200 bookings a second), the 10× rush and payment times are illustrative. Real sales also limit items per shopper and stop bots.

challenges.title: The last items
challenges.prompt: 500 items, 100 shoppers a second, and checkout reads the stock count, then writes it back minus one. Keep items sold twice at zero the whole time for 10 seconds.

predict.prompt: The stock count says 1. Two shoppers' checkouts both read 1 before either writes. What happens?

options.text: Both write 0 and both get the item: one item, two orders
options.explanation: Right. The second write overwrote the first, so one sale vanished from the count.

options.text: One of them is told it's sold out
options.explanation: Only if checking and taking happen in one atomic step.
Each writes back what it read minus one: 0, twice.

challenges.hint: Same fix as the train seats: what if checking and taking were one step?
challenges.explain: An atomic conditional update (take one only if one is left) can't interleave with another shopper's, so stock can't be sold twice.

challenges.title: Letting people in too fast
challenges.prompt: The waiting room is on but admits 300 shoppers a second, and the database handles about 200. At 2 seconds the sale opens with 10× the shoppers. Keep failed checkouts at 1% or less the whole time for 10 seconds.

predict.prompt: The waiting room lets 300 a second through to a database that handles 200. What happens to the extra 100 a second?

options.text: They fail at the database, as if there were no waiting room
options.explanation: Right. A waiting room only protects the database if it admits less than the database can handle.

options.text: Nothing: the waiting room protects the database
options.explanation: It only protects it at a rate the database can take.

options.text: They wait in the waiting room
options.explanation: They've already been let through it.

challenges.hint: What admit rate stays just under what the database can handle?
challenges.explain: Admitting a little under the database's capacity turns the rush into a queue instead of errors. Now look at the waiting time: that's the cost.

challenges.title: Letting people in too slowly
challenges.prompt: Now the waiting room admits only 100 a second. At 2 seconds the sale opens. Keep the slowest 5% of waits at 6 seconds or less, the whole time, for 10 seconds.
challenges.hint: The database could take more. How close to its capacity can you go without errors?
challenges.explain: Too slow wastes capacity and makes people wait; too fast causes errors. The best admit rate is just under what the database can handle, which is why real waiting rooms are tuned to the site's measured capacity.

critique.prompt: A proposal: checkout checks stock in a cache, then takes it in the database in a separate step; items stay reserved in carts until the shopper removes them; at 12:00 everyone hits checkout directly.

risks.text: Checking in one place and taking in another lets two shoppers buy the last item
risks.why: Check and take in one atomic step in the database.

risks.text: Reservations that never expire lock stock in carts nobody will check out
risks.why: Give each reservation an expiry, so unpaid items return to sale.

risks.text: Everyone hitting checkout at 12:00 overloads the database
risks.why: Put a waiting room in front that admits shoppers at a rate the database can handle.

risks.text: The sale page is served from a CDN
risks.why: Static pages from a CDN take load off the servers; that's good.

risks.text: Each order gets an ID before payment starts
risks.why: That's what makes payment retries safe (idempotency).

critique.hint: Think about the last item, shoppers who walk away, and the stroke of 12:00.

first.prompt: After the sale, more orders were confirmed than there were items. Which fix comes first?

options.text: Check and take stock in one atomic step
options.explanation: Right. Overselling means cancelling paid orders: the worst outcome for shoppers and the business.
That returns unpaid stock to sale; it doesn't stop overselling.
That protects the database; overselling would still happen at a lower rate.

critique.explain: Correctness before capacity: never sell what you don't have. Then expire reservations so stock isn't lost to abandoned carts, and add a waiting room tuned just under the database's capacity.

options.text: Shoppers who leave without paying would otherwise hold stock that real buyers want
options.explanation: Right. Too short, though, and buyers lose items mid-payment: it's a trade-off.
The point is returning abandoned stock, not pressure.

options.text: Databases can't store reservations for long
options.explanation: They can; the problem is stock nobody will buy.

quiz.prompt: What's the best rate for a waiting room to admit shoppers?

options.text: Just under what the checkout database can handle
options.explanation: Right. Faster causes errors; slower wastes capacity and makes people wait.

options.text: As slow as possible, to be safe
options.explanation: That makes waits longer than they need to be.
